title: Prioritize Tax-Advantaged Room Before Year-End
meta_description: Rank employer match, retirement, IRA, HSA and FSA opportunities by eligibility, deadline, liquidity and marginal household value before year-end.

sections.heading: Contribution Room Is an Option, Not an Obligation
paragraphs: An unused account limit can feel like a coupon about to expire. That feeling is dangerous when it turns a tax rule into a spending target. Contribution room is permission to shelter eligible money; it is not proof that contributing the maximum is affordable, suitable or more valuable than every competing use of cash.

The correct question is not “How do I fill every account?” It is “Which available dollar creates the strongest risk-adjusted household result?” An employer match may offer immediate value. A high-interest balance, overdue insurance premium or missing cash reserve may deserve priority before optional retirement contributions beyond that match.

Start with a household liquidity floor. List the next ninety days of essential bills, known irregular expenses and the minimum emergency reserve appropriate to job stability and dependents. Money committed to retirement accounts may face tax, penalty, plan or market constraints when withdrawn. Do not create a predictable cash crisis to obtain a tax advantage.

Tax-advantaged does not mean costless. Traditional contributions generally defer income tax rather than erase it; Roth contributions use after-tax dollars; HSA treatment depends on eligibility and qualified use; FSA balances can be subject to plan forfeiture rules. Fees, investment options and distribution restrictions also affect value.

The opening photograph shows an older couple reviewing documents because contribution decisions eventually meet real retirement needs. Anxiety is not a contribution strategy. A written order of operations can turn a large collection of limits, deadlines and plan notices into a manageable sequence.

Create an account inventory with owner, account type, custodian or employer, current-year contributions, employer money, remaining room, deadline, payroll cutoff and eligibility condition. Include a source for each number. A dashboard copied from last year can produce an excess contribution when limits or coverage changed.

Separate room from funding. Room is the legal or plan maximum still potentially available. Funding is cash the household can commit after near-term obligations. A person may have $20,000 of theoretical room and only $2,000 of prudent funding. The plan should allocate the $2,000, not shame the household for the difference.

Use tax estimates, not slogans. A deductible contribution’s current value depends on marginal tax circumstances, eligibility and future treatment. A credit may be more valuable than a deduction for an eligible saver. Obtain current tax advice for interactions with income-based benefits, credits or business deductions.

Set a decision date early enough for payroll and custodial processing. “December 31” is not the operational deadline when the final payroll election closes weeks earlier or a transfer needs settlement time. Write the institution’s cutoff beside the statutory deadline.

The year-end plan succeeds when valuable employer money is captured, eligible accounts are funded deliberately, liquidity remains intact and records prove the contribution year. Maximizing every published limit is not a requirement for a sound financial life.

Add a tax uncertainty flag to the inventory. Mark any account whose deduction, phase-out, coverage status or employer contribution is not yet confirmed. Allocate only the undisputed tier while clarification is pending. This preserves processing time without treating a guess as eligibility, and it gives a tax professional a concise list of decisions that require review.

sections.heading: Protect the Household Before Chasing the Tax Benefit
paragraphs: Build the funding hierarchy from consequences. First cover essential bills, required minimum payments and insurance needed to protect income and assets. Then preserve a cash buffer. After those protections, compare employer match, expensive debt, HSA or retirement opportunities and other goals using household facts.

A credit card charging a high annual rate creates a known drag that a market investment does not reliably overcome over a short horizon. Capturing a strong employer match can still rank first, but borrowing on the card to maximize an unmatched account usually exchanges certain cost for uncertain return.

Do not count an expected bonus, tax refund or asset sale before it arrives. Build a base plan from cash already available and a second plan activated only when contingent money clears. This prevents a contribution from forcing routine expenses onto debt.

Preserve sinking funds for known bills such as property tax, tuition, insurance, medical deductibles and vehicle repair. These are not emergencies merely because they occur irregularly. Moving their cash into a restricted account makes the balance sheet look optimized while weakening cash flow.

Match account horizon to goal. Retirement assets support long-duration needs; an HSA can support qualified medical spending and long-term saving; an FSA supports eligible expenses within plan rules. A home deposit due next year should not be routed into an account that makes timely access costly or uncertain.

Consider job and health risk together. A worker expecting a layoff, unpaid leave or major treatment may choose more cash even when room remains. Another household with stable income and a large reserve may accelerate contributions. The published limit does not know either situation.

Avoid using retirement loans or early distributions as the planned liquidity source. Plans differ, employment changes can affect repayment, and withdrawals can reduce long-term compounding or create tax consequences. An emergency option should not substitute for an emergency reserve.

Write a minimum viable contribution and an optional stretch amount. The minimum might earn the full employer match. The stretch amount can be funded from surplus after the next budget review. This two-level decision reduces all-or-nothing behavior.

If debt, liquidity and contributions compete closely, model three scenarios. Show cash at the next three month-ends, interest avoided, employer money received, estimated tax effect and account access. A one-page comparison is more useful than arguing whether investing or debt payoff is universally best.
The protection test passes when the contribution can occur without missed bills, new revolving debt or loss of essential coverage. Tax efficiency belongs inside a resilient plan, not above it.

sections.heading: Capture Employer Money with the Actual Match Formula
paragraphs: Employer contributions often deserve the first available retirement dollar, but “contribute to the match” is incomplete advice. Read the summary plan description and current election portal. Identify the match percentage, compensation definition, per-pay-period method, annual cap, vesting schedule and true-up provision.

A formula such as 50% of the first 6% of pay is not the same as a 6% match. Contributing 6% may earn 3% of eligible compensation. Bonuses may be included or excluded, and some employers make nonelective contributions regardless of employee deferral. Translate the formula into dollars.

Per-pay-period matching can punish front-loading if the plan lacks a year-end true-up. An employee who reaches the annual deferral limit before the final checks may receive no match on later payrolls. Confirm the plan’s mechanics before increasing the election sharply.

Vesting changes ownership, not the value of contributing today in every case. Employee deferrals are generally the employee’s, while employer money may vest over time. If departure is likely, review the schedule and plan terms rather than assuming the displayed employer balance is fully portable.

For 2026, the IRS basic elective-deferral limit for most 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans and the Thrift Savings Plan is $24,500. [[S1|The IRS limit announcement]] also states the general age-50 catch-up is $8,000, with a higher $11,250 limit for qualifying ages 60 through 63, subject to plan rules.

The employee deferral limit generally aggregates deferrals across relevant plans, including plans at unrelated employers. A job change does not automatically create a fresh full limit. Collect year-to-date payroll records from every employer and notify administrators promptly if an excess is possible.

Governmental 457(b) plans can have coordination rules different from 401(k) and 403(b) arrangements, and some 403(b) participants may have special service-based catch-ups. Do not infer one plan’s limit from another account label. Use the plan document and current official guidance.

Check whether the election can be changed for the remaining payrolls and when it becomes effective. Divide the desired additional deferral by remaining eligible checks, then test the resulting net pay against bills and benefit deductions. A mathematically valid percentage can still produce an unusable paycheck.
Retain the confirmation page and inspect the next pay statement. Verify the contribution, match and year-to-date total. A submitted election is not proof that payroll implemented it in time.

The employer-plan step is complete when the household understands the formula, captures the intended match, stays within shared limits and preserves enough net pay. “Maxed out” is less important than “implemented correctly.”

Review automatic escalation settings after the year-end change. A temporary high percentage can carry into January and unexpectedly reduce the first paycheck, while a manual reduction can disable a useful annual escalation feature. Record the intended first-payroll rate for the new year and confirm it after payroll resets year-to-date totals.

sections.heading: Turn Annual Limits into a Payroll Schedule
paragraphs: Annual limits become actionable only when converted into contributions per remaining paycheck. Start with the applicable limit, subtract all employee deferrals already made, subtract any scheduled deferrals that will occur without a change, and divide the intended remainder by checks that can still be modified.

For example, a worker under 50 who has deferred $18,500 toward a $24,500 limit has $6,000 of statutory room. If four eligible checks remain, filling it requires $1,500 per check, subject to compensation, plan and payroll constraints. That amount may be impractical even though room exists.

Use gross eligible pay, not take-home pay, when converting a percentage election. Payroll systems may cap the percentage or stop at the plan limit. Taxes, insurance, garnishments and other deductions determine whether the resulting net check can support the household.

Include Roth and pre-tax elective deferrals together where they share the same employee limit. Choosing tax treatment does not duplicate the room. After-tax employee contributions used in some plans may fall under a different overall limit, but they require explicit plan support and careful advice.

The overall defined-contribution limit includes employee deferrals, employer match, nonelective contributions and forfeiture allocations, while catch-up treatment can differ. [[S2|IRS contribution guidance]] lists a $72,000 general annual-additions limit for 2026, subject to compensation and plan rules. This is not a target for most employees.

Build a table by pay date with expected gross pay, deferral, employer contribution, cumulative employee deferral and estimated net pay. Mark bonus payroll separately. This catches the common mistake of applying a regular-pay percentage to compensation the plan excludes.

Leave a small operational buffer if year-to-date records are uncertain, then reconcile when final payroll data is available. Excess deferrals can require corrective distribution and create avoidable reporting work. Precision is more valuable than landing on the limit to the cent.

Coordinate spouses separately. Contribution limits and employer plans usually belong to each participant, while household cash is shared. One spouse’s superior match or lower-cost plan may receive the next dollar, but each person’s compensation, age, eligibility and existing contributions must be tracked individually.

If the required percentage is too high, fund the most valuable tier and stop. Missing optional room is not a penalty. Record the reason—liquidity, payroll cutoff or competing priority—and begin next year’s schedule earlier.

The payroll schedule passes when every planned deduction can be tied to a remaining check, match treatment is preserved and projected take-home pay stays positive and useful. A year-end scramble should become a monthly system next year.

sections.heading: Choose IRA Contributions by Eligibility and Tax Treatment
paragraphs: An IRA can extend retirement saving beyond a workplace plan, but the account label does not determine current tax treatment. Traditional IRA deductibility can phase out based on income and workplace coverage; Roth IRA eligibility can phase out based on modified adjusted gross income. Verify the current ranges before contributing.

For 2026, the combined traditional and Roth IRA contribution limit is $7,500, or $8,600 for an eligible person age 50 or older because the catch-up is $1,100. [[S1|The IRS announcement]] provides the current phase-out ranges. Contributions across both IRA types share the same personal limit.

Compensation requirements matter. A person generally needs eligible compensation, with spousal IRA rules potentially allowing contributions for a spouse on a joint return under the applicable limits. Investment income alone does not create unlimited IRA capacity.

A nondeductible traditional IRA contribution may be appropriate in some strategies, but it creates basis that must be tracked, generally on Form 8606. Existing pre-tax IRA balances can affect the tax calculation for a later conversion. Do not call the contribution “backdoor Roth” without modeling the full facts.

Roth versus traditional is a tax-timing decision, not a prediction contest. Compare the current marginal value, expected future taxable income, withdrawal flexibility, required distribution rules, state treatment and estate goals. Diversifying tax treatment can be reasonable when the future is uncertain.

IRA contributions for a tax year are generally possible through the return due date without extensions, but the custodian must code the year correctly. Select the contribution year deliberately and save the confirmation. A January deposit left coded to the new year may not repair the prior-year gap.

Do not delay solely because the investment choice is unfinished. Where appropriate, eligible cash can be contributed before the deadline and invested after a considered allocation decision. The account should still use a deliberate low-cost allocation rather than remaining forgotten in settlement cash.

Check fees, minimums and transfer timing before opening a new custodian relationship. A promotional bonus should not override investment cost, service quality, protection practices or the ability to document contribution year and tax forms.

The midpoint photograph shows tax documents and a calculator because the IRA decision belongs on the tax return as well as the investment statement. Contribution amount, deduction, credit eligibility, conversion and basis reporting must agree.

The IRA step passes when eligibility, compensation, shared limit, contribution year and tax reporting are documented. The best account type is the one whose rules and future treatment fit the household—not the one most praised online.

Confirm the account is actually an IRA and not merely a taxable brokerage account displayed beside it. Use the custodian’s contribution workflow, review the registration and avoid depositing more than intended. A purchase inside the wrong account cannot be relabeled as an IRA contribution simply because the same investment was selected.

sections.heading: Separate HSA Opportunity from FSA Forfeiture Risk
paragraphs: Health accounts require a different decision tree. An HSA is individually owned and can carry forward, but contributions require HSA eligibility. A health FSA is employer-sponsored and generally reimburses eligible expenses under plan rules, with possible grace-period or carryover features. Similar acronyms do not create interchangeable accounts.

For 2026, the HSA limit is $4,400 for self-only high-deductible health plan coverage and $8,750 for family coverage. [[S3|Revenue Procedure 2025-19]] provides those figures. Eligible individuals age 55 or older may have a $1,000 additional amount, and each spouse needing that addition generally needs a separate HSA.

HSA room is reduced by employer contributions, including qualifying cafeteria-plan amounts. Eligibility can change month by month with coverage, Medicare enrollment, dependent status or disqualifying other coverage. The last-month rule and testing period can create tax consequences if eligibility does not continue.

Payroll HSA contributions may avoid certain employment taxes when properly made through a cafeteria plan, while direct contributions may produce an income-tax deduction without the same payroll-tax effect. Compare methods but do not sacrifice eligibility or payroll timing for a theoretical advantage.

An HSA can reimburse current qualified medical expenses or preserve receipts for later reimbursement under current rules. That flexibility requires records: date, patient, provider, service, amount, proof of payment and proof that no other reimbursement or deduction occurred.

A health FSA election should begin with predictable eligible expenses, not the maximum. For plan years beginning in 2026, [[S4|IRS Publication 15-B]] states the employee salary-reduction limit is $3,400. The employer’s plan controls whether it offers a grace period or carryover and the applicable claims-submission deadline.

Use-or-lose exposure is a spending risk. Inventory unreimbursed eligible expenses, obtain necessary care based on health needs rather than balance anxiety, and submit claims with time to correct documentation. Do not buy unnecessary products merely to prevent forfeiture.

Coordinate HSA and FSA coverage carefully. A general-purpose health FSA can make an individual ineligible for HSA contributions, including in some cases coverage through a spouse. Limited-purpose or post-deductible arrangements may work differently. Confirm plan design before electing both.

Dependent-care assistance is separate from a health FSA and follows different eligibility, expense and limit rules. Do not merge balances on the year-end worksheet simply because both appear in the benefit portal.

The health-account step passes when eligibility is verified month by month, employer money is counted, claims deadlines are known and the contribution reflects expected care and cash flow. Tax preference must never drive unnecessary treatment or unsupported reimbursement.

sections.heading: Coordinate Self-Employment and Multiple Plans
paragraphs: Self-employment can create additional plan choices, but it also creates the easiest place to double-count limits. An employee deferral limit can follow the person across jobs, while employer contributions and annual-additions limits depend on plan and employer relationships. Related businesses require special analysis.

A solo 401(k), SEP IRA and SIMPLE IRA use different setup, election, contribution and filing rules. Choose based on business income, desired employee deferral, workforce, administrative burden and deadline—not the largest number in a comparison chart.

Net earnings from self-employment are not identical to gross business revenue. Contribution calculations can depend on deductible self-employment tax and plan contributions themselves. Use the current IRS worksheet or qualified professional rather than multiplying revenue by a headline percentage.

For 2026, the SIMPLE employee salary-reduction limit is $17,000, with a general $4,000 catch-up and a $5,250 higher catch-up for qualifying ages 60 through 63, subject to plan rules. [[S5|IRS small-business retirement guidance]] also explains employer contribution and timing requirements.

A worker who used the full employee deferral limit at a day job generally cannot make another full employee deferral to a solo 401(k), although an eligible business employer contribution may still be possible under the distinct limits. This is a calculation, not an account-opening shortcut.

SEP contributions do not create an employee salary-deferral election in the same way as a solo 401(k). A SEP can be administratively simpler, but existing employees, proportional contribution rules and IRA interactions can change the result. Model the actual business.

Plan establishment and contribution deadlines are not all the same. Some owner elections must exist by year-end even when funding can occur later. A tax-filing extension does not retroactively create every election. Record the setup date, election date and funding date separately.

Budget for required filings and administration. A one-participant 401(k) can trigger Form 5500-EZ filing requirements when assets cross the applicable threshold and at plan termination. Late administrative work can outweigh a small expected tax benefit.

If businesses share ownership or services, controlled-group and affiliated-service-group rules may affect who must be covered. This is professional-advice territory; opening separate plans does not make related employers unrelated.

The self-employed step passes when earned income supports the contribution, shared employee limits are reconciled, employer relationships are analyzed and every election and filing deadline is documented. Complexity should buy a material benefit.

Keep business and household cash decisions connected. A deductible employer contribution can still damage the business if payroll, sales tax, estimated tax or vendor obligations are unfunded. Prepare a post-contribution business cash forecast and obtain advice before moving money that may be needed to keep the operation solvent.

sections.heading: Use Deadlines as a Sequence, Not a Single Date
paragraphs: Year-end planning fails when every account is assigned December 31. Workplace deferrals depend on payroll; owner elections can have year-end requirements; IRA and HSA deposits may continue to the tax-return deadline; FSA spending and claim dates depend on the plan. Build a deadline ladder.

List four dates for each item: decision date, institution cutoff, legal or plan deadline and verification date. The decision date may be thirty days earlier than the formal deadline. The verification date is when the payroll statement or custodian confirms correct posting.

Prioritize irreversible deadlines. A missed final-payroll deferral usually cannot be recreated with a personal bank transfer to the 401(k). An IRA contribution may still be available later. Sequence scarce cash and administrative attention accordingly.

Age-based catch-ups require the correct age rule, plan permission and available compensation. The IRS states the general 2026 age-50 catch-up for most workplace plans is $8,000, while qualifying people who attain ages 60 through 63 can have an $11,250 higher amount. Confirm birth-year treatment and plan implementation.

Higher-income participants making catch-up contributions can face Roth catch-up requirements under current law and implementation guidance. Payroll systems and plan terms matter. Do not assume prior-year pre-tax treatment automatically continues.

Excess contributions are not extra room. If multiple employers, custodian coding or a mistaken election creates an excess, contact the administrator promptly. [[S2|IRS plan-limit guidance]] explains that excess deferrals generally require notice and corrective distribution by the specified following-year date.

Retain evidence in a year folder: final pay statements, W-2, custodian confirmations, Forms 5498 and 8889 where relevant, benefit elections, match formula, contribution-year coding and professional advice. Some forms arrive after the filing decision, so reconcile them when received.

The late-body photograph shows an older participant comparing documents at a laptop. Catch-up rules can be valuable, but their age bands and plan conditions require exact reading. The image belongs here because verification—not urgency—is the final-stage task.

Create reminders for open enrollment, first payroll, midyear reconciliation, the final election cutoff and tax-filing season. The best fix for year-end pressure is to distribute decisions across the year.

The deadline step passes when every contribution has an owner, source account, amount, cutoff and confirmation. If an institution cannot process in time, document the missed room and protect the cash rather than using a rushed or ineligible workaround.

Never wait for a missing tax form to identify the basic facts already available in payroll and account records. Reconcile preliminary totals, flag the form for later comparison and delay filing when necessary. Filing early is not valuable if it locks an avoidable contribution or reporting error into the return.

sections.heading: Approve the Next Dollar with a Written Ranking
paragraphs: Bring every eligible account into one ranking instead of maximizing them in isolation. A practical order can begin with required bills and reserve, then full employer match, then high-cost debt, then HSA or retirement opportunities, then taxable goals. The exact order changes with household facts.

For each next dollar, record immediate employer money, estimated current tax effect, access restrictions, fees, investment quality, expected holding period and risk reduced. Score ranges are useful only when the assumptions remain visible.

Consider the Saver’s Credit for eligible contributors. For 2026, IRS materials list income ceilings of $80,500 for married filing jointly, $60,375 for head of household and $40,250 for other eligible filing statuses, with the actual credit depending on detailed rules. A credit can change the ranking materially.

Avoid false precision in long-term growth projections. The immediate match and known fees can be measured; market return and future tax rate cannot. Use a range and test whether the decision still works under lower return or different tax assumptions.

Choose the amount, not just the account. An extra $1,000 may earn the remainder of a match; the next $1,000 may have only tax deferral. Marginal value changes at thresholds, so rank contributions in tiers.

Submit changes one at a time and save confirmation. Check payroll, bank settlement and custodian coding. If a transfer fails, a screenshot of the instruction does not establish a completed contribution.

After funding, set an investment allocation appropriate to the account and goal. Contribution room without an investment decision can leave retirement money in cash unintentionally. Review expense ratios, diversification and risk rather than chasing recent winners.

Update beneficiaries and contact details while accounts are open. Contribution optimization cannot compensate for stale ownership instructions, inaccessible credentials or missing household records. Store a secure account inventory that a trusted person can locate.

Write the reason for any unused room. “Protected emergency reserve,” “missed payroll cutoff,” “income eligibility uncertain” and “paid 24% debt” are decisions, not failures. The note improves next year’s process.

The final approval is simple: fund the highest-value eligible tier that preserves liquidity, verify it, and stop when the next dollar no longer beats the household’s alternative. Account limits are boundaries; priorities determine the plan.

Schedule a January postmortem. Compare planned and actual amounts, missed matches, processing delays, tax forms and cash strain. Convert the successful year-end amounts into automatic per-paycheck or monthly targets. The purpose is not to repeat a sprint; it is to make the next contribution cycle quieter, earlier and easier to verify.

summary: Contribution room is permission to use a tax-advantaged account, not an instruction to reach every maximum. Start with essential bills, minimum debt payments, insurance and a liquidity floor. Calculate how much cash is genuinely available before comparing accounts.

Create an inventory for each owner and account: current contribution, employer money, remaining room, eligibility condition, legal deadline, payroll or custodian cutoff and verification date. Use current official limits and plan documents rather than last year’s dashboard.

Capture employer money deliberately. Translate the match formula into dollars, check eligible compensation, vesting, per-pay-period treatment and any true-up. Front-loading can reduce matching in plans without a true-up, so model every remaining check.

For 2026, the basic employee deferral limit for most 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans and the Thrift Savings Plan is $24,500. The general age-50 catch-up is $8,000; qualifying ages 60 through 63 may have an $11,250 higher catch-up, subject to plan rules.

Convert the desired year-end amount into deductions per remaining payroll. Include deferrals made at prior employers, traditional and Roth amounts sharing the employee limit, bonuses and projected net pay. Inspect the next pay statement after every change.

The 2026 combined traditional and Roth IRA limit is $7,500, or $8,600 for an eligible person age 50 or older. Verify compensation, deduction and Roth eligibility. Track nondeductible basis and designate the contribution year correctly.

For 2026, HSA limits are $4,400 for eligible self-only coverage and $8,750 for eligible family coverage, plus a potential $1,000 age-55 amount. Count employer deposits and confirm month-by-month eligibility, Medicare and other coverage.

Health FSAs are not HSAs. The 2026 employee salary-reduction limit is $3,400, but the employer plan controls any carryover, grace period and claim deadline. Elect from expected qualified expenses and avoid unnecessary spending to prevent forfeiture.

Self-employed people must coordinate personal deferral limits across jobs and calculate employer contributions from eligible earnings, not revenue. Solo 401(k), SEP and SIMPLE arrangements have different establishment, election, funding and filing rules.

Build a deadline ladder with decision, processing, legal and verification dates. Workplace payroll often closes first; IRA and HSA funding may remain available through the tax-return deadline. Never assume all opportunities end on December 31.

Retain pay statements, election confirmations, plan terms, custodian receipts and tax forms. Contact administrators quickly about potential excess contributions. A completed transfer must also be coded to the correct owner, account and tax year.

Rank the next dollar in tiers: liquidity protection, employer match, expensive debt, health and retirement opportunities, then other goals as facts support. Fund the highest-value eligible tier, verify it and stop when the next dollar has a better household use.

Mark uncertain items rather than guessing. Deduction eligibility, Roth phase-outs, HSA coverage, related businesses and catch-up implementation can require current professional or plan guidance. Fund only the confirmed tier while questions are resolved and retain the answer with the account records.

After a temporary payroll increase, check the next-year election. Automatic escalation, plan resets and a high percentage carried into January can change net pay unexpectedly. Record the intended first-payroll rate and verify both employee and employer amounts on the statement.

Complete a January postmortem. Compare the worksheet with actual deposits, matching, contribution-year coding, forms and household cash. Turn successful year-end amounts into realistic monthly or per-paycheck targets so the next cycle relies less on deadlines and more on routine verification.

Do not file from memory when contribution forms arrive later. Reconcile preliminary payroll and custodian totals, retain the worksheet and compare every later form. Correct an institution error promptly and delay filing when necessary; speed is not an advantage when account ownership, amount or tax-year coding remains unresolved.

faq.question: Should every available account be maxed before year-end?
faq.answer: No. Preserve essential cash, insurance and debt obligations, then rank eligible contribution tiers by household value.

faq.question: Can a bank transfer replace a missed 401(k) payroll deferral?
faq.answer: Usually employee elective deferrals must run through eligible payroll, so confirm the plan cutoff early.

faq.question: Do Roth and traditional 401(k) deferrals have separate limits?
faq.answer: They generally share the employee elective-deferral limit, though plan and overall contribution rules also apply.

faq.question: How late can an IRA contribution be made?
faq.answer: Generally through the return due date without extensions, with enough processing time and correct tax-year coding.

faq.question: Does employer money reduce HSA room?
faq.answer: Yes. Eligible employer and cafeteria-plan HSA contributions count toward the applicable annual limit.

faq.question: What should be kept after contributing?
faq.answer: Keep election confirmations, pay statements, custodian receipts, year designation, plan terms and relevant tax forms.

glossary.definition: The unused portion of an applicable legal or plan contribution limit.
Compensation an employee elects to direct to an eligible employer retirement plan.
An employer contribution determined by the employee contribution and plan formula.
A plan feature that may reconcile employer matching across the full plan year.
Additional contribution capacity potentially available by age and plan rules.
Specified employee and employer amounts counted toward a defined-contribution plan’s overall limit.
An income measure adjusted under account-specific tax rules for eligibility or phase-outs.
The tax year to which a custodian or plan applies an eligible contribution.
A required period of continued HSA eligibility after use of certain contribution rules.
